title: Parish and Witness
premise: August Lockridge, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory borders on a curse, is hired to close the file on Edith Marlow, a parish organist who vanished eleven years ago. When August discovers her recovered diary contains entries written after her disappearance, they realize the diary is a coded ledger recording payments made to powerful townspeople of Ashcombe Fen—and that whoever kept writing in it is still alive, still watching, and still collecting. As August's perfect recall begins to betray them, inserting memories that never happened, they must untangle which recollections are real before the ledger's final entry names them. In the end August exposes the parish council's decades of buried crimes, but chooses to burn the original ledger, keeping only the memory—because in Ashcombe, belonging has always cost more than truth.
about_author: Ansel Dunmore is the pen name of a former parish clerk from the East Anglian fens who spent fifteen years archiving village records before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about small communities where everyone remembers everything and no one says anything.

chapters.title: The File That Would Not Close
chapters.summary: POV August. Insurance investigator August Lockridge takes the Marlow missing-person file as a favor to an old colleague, expecting routine paperwork. In the evidence box, Edith's diary sits alongside a coroner's note marked 'no body, no closure.' The emotional beat is restless professional curiosity—August can't stop reading, and the last entry is dated nine days after Edith vanished.

chapters.title: Ink After the End
chapters.summary: POV August. August compares handwriting samples and confirms the post-disappearance entries are Edith's own—flawless penmanship, but describing a harvest festival that happened a year after she was last seen. August's photographic memory flags a detail: the festival photo in the parish newsletter shows someone wearing Edith's coat. The beat is the first true chill.

chapters.title: Ashcombe Fen
chapters.summary: POV August. August arrives in the village: a drowned landscape of drainage dikes, a squat Norman church, and a community that closes ranks the moment the word 'insurance' is spoken. The vicar, Ruth Calloway, is warm but evasive; the churchwarden, Gerald Pike, is openly hostile. Beat: the sense of being watched by an entire village at once.

chapters.title: The Organist's Loft
chapters.summary: POV August. Given access to the church, August climbs to the organ loft where Edith practiced and finds pencil marks on the pipe casings—numbers, dates, initials. Cross-referencing with the diary, August realizes the marks are an index. Beat: the thrill of the hunt, undercut when August recalls a conversation with Pike that August cannot actually remember having.

chapters.title: What August Remembers
chapters.summary: POV August, with a flashback interlude. For the first time, August doubts their own memory: a vivid recollection of Edith alive at a bus stop, which cannot be real, sits in their mind with photographic certainty. August begins keeping a written journal against their own mind. Beat: fear of self-betrayal.

chapters.title: The Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: POV August. The diary's 'diary' entries decode into a payment ledger: sums, dates, and initials matching parish council members, stretching back thirty years. Edith wasn't recording her life; she was recording their debts. Beat: the intoxication of cracking the code, followed by the weight of what it implies.

chapters.title: Debts of the Parish
chapters.summary: POV August, alternating with Ruth. August traces the earliest entries to a 1990s land deal that flooded neighboring farms—Ashcombe's prosperity was bought with someone else's ruin. Ruth, pressed, admits Edith came to her a week before disappearing, frightened. Beat: Ruth's guilt and August's growing sense that everyone is a debtor or a creditor.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wears the Coat
chapters.summary: POV August. August identifies the figure in Edith's coat from the festival photo: Silas Wren, the council's surveyor, who has never missed a harvest festival in forty years. Following Wren at dusk along the dikes, August sees him leave an envelope in a hollow willow. Beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Hollow Willow
chapters.summary: POV August. The envelope contains cash and a fresh index card in Edith's handwriting—dated this month. Someone is still paying, and someone with Edith's hand is still receiving. August photographs everything, then finds their own car's tire slashed. Beat: the investigation turns personal.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Sundays
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. Ruth's chapter: her memory of Edith—brilliant, bitter, in love with the village and excluded from it. Ruth confesses to the reader (not to August) that she saw Edith the night she vanished and said nothing, because Edith asked her to. Beat: complicity as a form of love.

chapters.title: A Memory of Rain
chapters.summary: POV August. August's false memories multiply: a funeral, a flood, a woman's voice singing the parish hymn. Each is vivid, dated, and impossible. August realizes the diary's later entries are written to implant themselves—Edith, or whoever writes as Edith, is editing August's mind through the text. Beat: psychological vertigo.

chapters.title: The Drowned Farm
chapters.summary: POV August. Following the ledger's oldest entry, August walks to the flooded farmstead of the Hollis family, ruined by the land deal. In the collapsed barn: a second diary, earlier, rougher—Edith's first draft, naming not debts but crimes. Beat: pity and fury fused.

chapters.title: Silas Speaks
chapters.summary: POV August. Confronted, Wren doesn't deny the payments; he defends them. 'Every parish runs on what it prefers not to know,' he says, and warns August that the last person who tried to balance the books drowned. Beat: the seductive logic of corruption, delivered calmly over tea.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: POV August. August dredges the fen-adjacent drainage culvert named in the draft diary and finds Edith's bicycle—rusted, submerged, but no body. The evidence says she went into the water; the living diary says she didn't die. Both can be true. Beat: the mystery pivots from 'what happened' to 'who is writing.'

chapters.title: The Understudy
chapters.summary: POV August. August identifies a candidate: Naomi Hollis, the drowned farmers' daughter, raised in the church choir under Edith's tutelage—close enough to forge her hand, motivated enough to keep the ledger alive. But when August finds Naomi, she is terrified, not defiant: 'She told me to give it to you when you were ready.' Beat: the hunter realizes they were invited.

chapters.title: Invitation
chapters.summary: POV August. The diary's newest entry, in Edith's hand, is addressed to August by name and directs them to the organ loft at midnight. August understands the whole investigation has been choreographed—by Edith, if Edith lives. Beat: the trap and the gift are the same shape.

chapters.title: Midnight in the Loft
chapters.summary: POV August. At the appointed hour, Edith Marlow—older, half-crippled, unmistakably alive—steps from behind the organ pipes. She faked her death to become the ledger's invisible witness, and she has spent years choosing her successor. She offers August the book: 'Keep it, or end it.' Beat: awe and terror at the scale of her patience.

chapters.title: The Price of Belonging
chapters.summary: POV August. Edith tells the whole story: the land deal, the deaths covered up, why she couldn't stay and couldn't leave. She chose August because a perfect memory is the only vault no one can bribe. But August has noticed the flaw—Edith's recent entries contain errors, and Edith's mind is going the way the diary always said it wouldn't. Beat: tragic tenderness.

chapters.title: Every Debtor Assembled
chapters.summary: POV August. August calls a parish council meeting and, from memory alone, recites thirty years of payments, dates, and initials before the whole village—no documents, no denials. Pike breaks; Wren calculates; Ruth weeps. Beat: the climax—memory weaponized into witness, the title's two halves made one.

chapters.title: What the Fire Takes
chapters.summary: POV August. With the police en route and confessions in the air, August faces the choice Edith offered. The ledger, burned, frees the village from its past; kept, it only appoints a new jailer. August burns it in the churchyard brazier, keeping nothing but recall. Edith watches, finally off the record. Beat: catharsis through renunciation.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: POV August. Weeks later, the case closed and Edith quietly relocated, August writes their own final diary entry—the first thing they've ever chosen to write down rather than merely remember. Some things should outlive memory; some should live only in it. Beat: peace, and the decision to stay in Ashcombe a while longer.

chapters.title: Parish and Witness
chapters.summary: POV August, coda. At the next harvest festival, August stands at the back of the church as the hymn rises, no longer investigator but neighbor. On the organ, someone plays Edith's arrangement; in August's mind, every note is preserved exactly. The village belongs to those who remember it—and August, at last, belongs to the village. Beat: belonging earned, memory redeemed.
